newsitem.title: UK: TENNIS-WILANDER, NOVACEK DROP FIGHT AGAINST DOPING BAN.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-WILANDER, NOVACEK DROP FIGHT AGAINST DOPING BAN.

text.p: Former world number one Mats Wilander and fellow veteran Karel Novacek dropped their fight against a doping ban on Wednesday, two years after testing positive for cocaine.
The International Tennis Federation (ITF) immediately banned the pair for three months and ordered them to forfeit prize money and ranking points earned in the past two years.

The ITF said Wilander, three times French Open champion, and Novacek had accepted the positive results of doping tests carried out at Roland Garros in 1995 but contended the cocaine had been consumed unwittingly.
Wilander and Novacek had dropped a legal case against the federation which had been due to come before the London High Court next month, it said.
"Mr Wilander and Mr Novacek state that they were unaware of the presence of cocaine in their bodies and believe that the cocaine was unknowingly consumed," the ITF said in a statement.
"They acknowledge the identity of the urine samples in question as their own and they acknowledge the positive results from the 1995 French Open."
The ban will have little effect as neither Wilander, who also won the Australian Open three times and the U.S. Open once, nor Novacek has played much on the ATP Tour recently.

But Wilander, a former Davis Cup player for Sweden and world number one in 1988, will lose $289,005 in prize money earned since June 1995. Czech Novacek, a U.S. Open semifinalist in 1994, must return $185,765.
Wilander, now 32, won 33 singles titles during his career but played in only 13 tournaments last year and had a mere 44 ranking points to his name before Wednesday's announcement.

Novacek, also 32 and a former Davis Cup competitor, had played mostly doubles since his last appearance in a Grand Slam event in 1995 and had only three points in singles in the most recent ATP rankings list.
In January Spaniard Ignacio Truyol became the first tennis player to be suspended for doping when he received a one-year ban.

The ATP declined to name the substances found in Truyol's sample but said they fell into its class I -- which includes steroids and masking agents -- and class II -- stimulants and narcotic analgesics.
Wilander and Novacek were given random tests in Paris in June 1995 but the results did not become public until a British newspaper broke the story seven months later.
